sections.subtitle: ASK/RPK/RASK/unit cost are management's own KPIs for capacity, traffic and margin -- annual only, not disclosed at the half-year

charts.annotation: UnderlyingPBT is only disclosed from FY2025; earlier years show statutory net income alone.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF

capacityTraffic.title: Capacity vs traffic
capacityTraffic.content:
ASK (Available Seat Kilometres) is capacity flown -- seats multiplied by distance; RPK (Revenue Passenger Kilometres) is traffic actually carried -- paying passengers multiplied by distance.

For Qantas Airways Limited: ASK growing faster than RPK means capacity is being added ahead of demand, which pressures load factor and RASK; the gap between the two bars is the load-factor story shown in the next chart.

What to watch:

  • ASK growth outpacing RPK growth for several periods in a row
  • Capacity discipline versus competitors (Virgin, international carriers) on key routes

loadFactor.title: Seat factor (load factor)
loadFactor.content:
Seat factor is RPK ÷ ASK -- the percentage of available seats actually sold. It is the single most-watched operating KPI in the airline industry.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the group runs in the low-to-mid 80s%; a sustained fall below that band, especially alongside rising ASK, signals overcapacity rather than a soft market.

What to watch:

  • Seat factor trending down while capacity (ASK) keeps growing
  • Seasonal dips (H1 is typically softer than H2) -- only shown here on an FY basis since Qantas does not disclose it at the half-year

unitEconomics.title: RASK and unit cost
unitEconomics.content:
RASK is revenue per Available Seat Kilometre (A$ cents); unit cost is total operating cost per ASK. The spread between the two lines is the operating margin per seat-kilometre flown.

For Qantas Airways Limited: unit cost rose from ~9.7c (FY2024) to ~14.8c (FY2026) on fuel and labour inflation while RASK only partly kept pace -- the spread narrowing is the margin pressure visible in the EBITDA-margin chart above.

What to watch:

  • Unit cost rising faster than RASK (margin compression)
  • Fuel price and FX moves, the two biggest swing factors in unit cost

underlyingPbt.title: Underlying PBT vs statutory net income
underlyingPbt.content:
Underlying PBT is Qantas's own non-statutory earnings measure -- profit before tax adjusted to strip out items management judges one-off or non-operating (e.g. impairments, transformation costs, AASB 16 lease timing). Statutory net income is the audited, unadjusted GAAP figure.

For Qantas Airways Limited: management guides the market to Underlying PBT, not statutory profit, so a widening gap between the two is worth asking what is being excluded and whether it recurs. Only disclosed from FY2025 onward in the data captured here.

What to watch:

  • Items excluded from Underlying PBT that show up again in a later period (not really one-off)
  • Underlying PBT growing while statutory net income shrinks, or vice versa

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Qantas Airways Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Qantas Airways Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Qantas Airways Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Qantas Airways Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Qantas Airways Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
